o: has denticulate ligament attaching down to S2 level

The denticulate ligament is formed by pia mater, not dura, and its lowest denticulation is at the L1 root (Last's). It is the dural sac that ends at S2.
The statement mixes up two structures.
is a prolongation of the inner layer of the dura mater of the posterior cranial fossa

Last's says the spinal dura is the inner (meningeal) layer of the posterior fossa dura continued through the foramen magnum. The outer (periosteal) layer does not continue below the foramen.
That is why the spinal canal has an epidural space.
is attached to the spinal arachnoid by web-like processes which are well developed to form an anterior median septum

The web-like strands run from the arachnoid to the pia, not from the dura, and they form an incomplete posterior median septum, not an anterior one.
Two errors in one statement.
is surrounded by a layer of fat in which lies the internal vertebral venous plexus

The spinal dura is surrounded by the extradural (epidural) space, which contains fat and the internal vertebral venous plexus.
This is the space used for epidural anaesthesia. Answer B: 2 and 4.
It has no body

The atlas has no body; its body has fused with the axis to form the dens.
It is a ring of anterior and posterior arches with lateral masses.
The vertebral artery grooves the upper surface of its posterior arch

The vertebral artery grooves the upper surface of the posterior arch of the atlas behind the lateral mass, with the C1 nerve (suboccipital nerve) below it.
The groove may be bridged by bone (ponticulus posticus).
Its transverse process is palpable between the mastoid process and the angle of the mandible

The tip of the large transverse process of the atlas is palpable between the mastoid process and the angle of the mandible.
XI crosses it.
The transverse ligament attaches to the anterior tubercle

The transverse ligament attaches to tubercles on the medial sides of the lateral masses, holding the dens against the anterior arch. The anterior tubercle gives attachment to longus colli.
Rupture of the transverse ligament allows the dens to compress the cord.

questions.s: Regarding the ligaments of the craniovertebral junction:
o: The apical ligament of the dens is a remnant of the notochord

The apical ligament of the dens, running from its tip to the anterior margin of the foramen magnum, is a remnant of the notochord.
It is weak and of little mechanical importance.
The alar ligaments attach the dens to the medial sides of the occipital condyles and limit rotation

The alar ligaments attach the sides of the dens to the medial sides of the occipital condyles. They are strong and check rotation and lateral flexion of the head.
Their injury can cause atlanto-axial rotatory instability.
The tectorial membrane is the upward continuation of the anterior longitudinal ligament

The tectorial membrane is the upward continuation of the posterior longitudinal ligament to the basiocciput. The anterior longitudinal ligament continues as the anterior atlanto-occipital membrane.
Posterior to posterior.
The vertebral artery pierces the posterior atlanto-occipital membrane

The vertebral artery (with the C1 nerve) pierces, or passes beneath the lower free border of, the posterior atlanto-occipital membrane to enter the vertebral canal.
The membrane may ossify to form a ponticulus posticus.

questions.s: Concerning movements of the craniovertebral joints:
o: Flexion and extension of the head occur mainly at the atlanto-occipital joints

Last's says the atlanto-occipital joints allow nodding (flexion and extension) and some lateral flexion, but no rotation, because the condyles form an egg-shaped ball.
"Yes" movements.
Rotation of the head occurs mainly at the atlanto-axial joints

Rotation of the head occurs mainly at the atlanto-axial joints, where the atlas and skull rotate on the axis around the dens.
"No" movements.
The atlanto-axial joints comprise one median and two lateral synovial joints

The atlanto-axial joints comprise one median joint (dens with the anterior arch and transverse ligament) and two lateral joints between the lateral masses. All are synovial.
Three joints act together.
There is an intervertebral disc between the atlas and the axis

There is no intervertebral disc between C1 and C2, or between the occiput and C1. The first disc is at C2/3.
Answer C: 1, 2 and 3.
The vertebral artery usually enters the foramen transversarium of C6

The vertebral artery usually enters the foramen transversarium of C6. The foramen of C7 usually transmits only the vertebral vein (and sometimes an accessory vein).
So C7's foramen is small or absent.
The anterior tubercle of the transverse process of C6 is the carotid tubercle

The anterior tubercle of the C6 transverse process is the carotid (Chassaignac's) tubercle. The common carotid can be compressed against it, and it is a landmark for stellate ganglion block.
The inferior thyroid artery arches near it.
Uncovertebral joints occur between C1 and C2

Last's says the uncus on the upper surface of the bodies of C3 to T1 may appear to form a joint (of Luschka) because a small cavity develops; these are degenerative, not true synovial joints, and they do not occur between C1 and C2.
The atlas and axis have no bodies to form them.
The spines of C3 to C6 are usually bifid

The spines of C3 to C6 (and usually C2) are bifid. C7, the vertebra prominens, has a long non-bifid spine.
C7 is the first easily palpable spine.
The head of a typical rib articulates with the bodies of its own and the vertebra above

The head of a typical rib articulates with the bodies of its own vertebra and the one above, hence the demifacets on typical thoracic vertebrae.
The crest of the head is attached to the disc between them.
The first rib articulates with T1 only

The first rib articulates with T1 only; T1 has a complete facet for rib 1 and a demifacet for rib 2.
Ribs 1, 10, 11 and 12 articulate with one vertebra.
The tubercle of a typical rib articulates with the transverse process of the vertebra of the same number

The tubercle of a typical rib articulates with the transverse process of the vertebra of the same number. For example, rib 6 articulates with the bodies of T5 and T6 and the transverse process of T6.
The costotransverse joint.
The 11th and 12th ribs articulate with the transverse processes of their own vertebrae

Ribs 11 and 12 have no tubercles and no costotransverse joints.
Answer C: 1, 2 and 3.

questions.s: Regarding the lumbar vertebrae and sacrum:
o: The mammillary process is on the posterior border of the superior articular process

The mammillary process lies on the posterior border of the superior articular process of a lumbar vertebra. It gives attachment to multifidus.
Accessory processes lie at the root of the transverse process.
The iliolumbar ligament attaches to the transverse process of L5

The iliolumbar ligament runs from the tip of the L5 transverse process to the iliac crest.
It stabilises the lumbosacral junction.
The sacral hiatus results from failure of fusion of the laminae of S5

The sacral hiatus results from failure of fusion of the laminae of S5 (sometimes S4 too). It is bounded by the sacral cornua and used for caudal epidural injection.
It is covered by the superficial posterior sacrococcygeal ligament.
The dural sac in the adult ends at the level of L5

In the adult the dural (and arachnoid) sac ends at about S2, not L5.
The cord ends at about L1/L2.

questions.s: Concerning the intervertebral discs and ligaments:
o: The nucleus pulposus is derived from the notochord

The nucleus pulposus is a notochordal remnant. The annulus fibrosus comes from sclerotome.
Chordomas arise from notochordal remnants.
A posterolateral L4/5 disc protrusion usually compresses the L5 nerve root

Last's rule: a posterolateral disc herniation irritates the root one below the disc (L4/5 disc to L5 root, L5/S1 disc to S1 root, C6/7 disc to C7 root). The root of the same number has already left, hugging its pedicle.
A far lateral herniation affects the exiting root instead.
The ligamentum flavum is composed mainly of collagen

The ligamenta flava are composed mainly of yellow elastic tissue, not collagen.
That elasticity helps restore the spine after flexion.
The posterior longitudinal ligament is broad over the vertebral bodies and narrow over the discs

The posterior longitudinal ligament is narrow over the vertebral bodies (where basivertebral veins exit) and broad, denticulate and attached over the discs.
Its weakness posterolaterally favours posterolateral herniation.
There are 31 pairs: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and 1 coccygeal

There are 31 pairs of spinal nerves: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and 1 coccygeal.
There are 8 cervical nerves but 7 cervical vertebrae.
The C5 nerve emerges between C5 and C6 vertebrae

Cervical nerves C1 to C7 emerge above their vertebrae, so C5 emerges between C4 and C5. C8 emerges between C7 and T1.
Below that, each nerve emerges below its vertebra.
The dorsal root ganglion lies in the intervertebral foramen

The dorsal root ganglion lies in the intervertebral foramen, except for the sacral and coccygeal nerves, whose ganglia lie in the sacral canal.
Foraminal stenosis can compress it.
The dorsal root ganglion contains synapses between primary and secondary sensory neurones

The dorsal root ganglion contains pseudounipolar cell bodies but no synapses.
The first synapse is in the cord or brainstem.

questions.s: Concerning the posterior (dorsal) rami of spinal nerves:
o: The dorsal ramus of C1 has no cutaneous branch

The dorsal ramus of C1 (suboccipital nerve) has no cutaneous branch; it is purely motor to the suboccipital muscles.
So there is no C1 dermatome.
The dorsal rami of C7, C8, L4 and L5 usually do not reach the skin

Last's says the dorsal rami of C7, C8, L4 and L5 usually do not reach the skin.
They supply only muscle.
Dorsal rami supply the skin of the posterior surface of the upper limb

No dorsal ramus ever supplies the skin or muscle of a limb.
Limbs are supplied entirely by anterior rami.
In the upper half of the body the medial branch reaches the skin

In the upper half of the body the medial branches of the dorsal rami reach the skin; in the lower half it is the lateral branches.
A Last's principle of back innervation.
It is bounded by rectus capitis posterior major, obliquus capitis superior and obliquus capitis inferior

The suboccipital triangle is bounded by rectus capitis posterior major (medially), obliquus capitis superior (laterally above) and obliquus capitis inferior (below).
It lies deep to semispinalis capitis.
Its floor is formed by the posterior atlanto-occipital membrane and posterior arch of atlas

The floor of the triangle is formed by the posterior atlanto-occipital membrane and the posterior arch of the atlas, with the vertebral artery on the arch.
A landmark in posterior approaches.
The greater occipital nerve is the dorsal ramus of C1

The greater occipital nerve is the medial branch of the dorsal ramus of C2. It winds around the lower border of obliquus inferior and pierces semispinalis capitis and trapezius.
The dorsal ramus of C1 is the suboccipital nerve.
The suboccipital nerve supplies all the muscles bounding the triangle and rectus capitis posterior minor

The suboccipital nerve (dorsal ramus of C1) supplies all the muscles bounding the triangle and rectus capitis posterior minor, and part of semispinalis capitis.
It emerges between the vertebral artery and the arch.
Includes multifidus

Multifidus belongs to the transversospinalis group, deep to erector spinae.
Erector spinae is iliocostalis, longissimus and spinalis.
Is supplied by anterior rami

All the intrinsic (deep) back muscles, including erector spinae, are supplied by posterior (dorsal) rami.
That is how they are defined.
Has spinalis as its most lateral column

Iliocostalis is the lateral column, longissimus intermediate and spinalis medial.
"I Love Spaghetti" from lateral to medial.
Arises from a common origin on the sacrum, iliac crest and lumbar spines

Last's says erector spinae arises from a thick tendon on the sacrum, iliac crest and lumbar spines, deep to the lumbar fascia, then diverges into its columns.
Answer D: 4 only.
Extends from the external occipital protuberance to the spine of C7

The ligamentum nuchae is a median fibrous septum from the external occipital protuberance and crest to the spine of C7, attached to the cervical spines.
It separates the muscles of the two sides.
Gives origin to trapezius

The ligamentum nuchae gives origin to trapezius, and also to splenius capitis, rhomboid minor and serratus posterior superior.
Its role is mainly for muscle attachment in humans.
Gives origin to levator scapulae

Levator scapulae arises from the transverse processes of C1 to C4, not the ligamentum nuchae.
It lies more laterally.
Is homologous with the supraspinous ligament

The ligamentum nuchae is homologous with the supraspinous ligament, which it continues above C7.
In grazing animals it is thick and elastic.
Lies in the extradural space

The internal vertebral venous plexus lies in the extradural (epidural) space, in the fat between the dura and bone.
It can bleed in spinal surgery.
Is valveless

The plexus is valveless, so it provides a route for metastasis, for example from the prostate to the vertebrae and skull.
Batson's plexus.
Communicates with the cranial dural venous sinuses through the foramen magnum

The plexus communicates with the cranial dural venous sinuses (basilar plexus and occipital sinus) through the foramen magnum.
A continuous valveless system from pelvis to skull.
Receives the basivertebral veins from the vertebral bodies

The plexus receives the basivertebral veins, which emerge from the back of each vertebral body beneath the posterior longitudinal ligament.
All four true: E.

questions.s: In a lumbar puncture in an adult:
o: The line joining the highest points of the iliac crests usually crosses the L4 spine or the L4/5 interspace

The line joining the highest points of the iliac crests (Tuffier's or the intercristal line) usually crosses the L4 spine or the L4/5 interspace.
It is the main landmark for lumbar puncture.
The needle passes through the ligamentum flavum before the epidural space

The needle passes skin, subcutaneous tissue, supraspinous ligament, interspinous ligament and ligamentum flavum, then the epidural space, dura and arachnoid.
The ligamentum flavum gives a distinct "give".
The needle must penetrate the pia mater to enter the subarachnoid space

The subarachnoid space lies between the arachnoid and the pia; the pia invests the cord and roots and is not pierced.
CSF flows once the arachnoid is breached.
Puncture at L1/2 is safe because the cord ends at L3

The adult cord usually ends at about L1/2, so lumbar puncture is performed at L3/4 or L4/5. The L3 level applies at birth.
Puncture at L1/2 risks the conus.
C6 supplies the thumb

C6 supplies the lateral forearm and thumb. C7 supplies the middle finger and C8 the little finger.
A C6 radiculopathy causes thumb numbness.
T10 supplies the umbilicus

T10 supplies the skin at the level of the umbilicus. T4/5 is at the nipple and T7 at the subcostal angle.
Useful for sensory levels.
L4 supplies the medial side of the leg

L4 supplies the medial side of the leg and the region of the medial malleolus.
L5 supplies the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot.
S1 supplies the skin over the medial malleolus

S1 supplies the lateral ankle, the lateral dorsum and sole of the foot and the little toe, not the medial malleolus.
The medial malleolus is L4.
An axial line is a junction between dermatomes supplied from discontinuous spinal levels

An axial line is a junction between dermatomes supplied from discontinuous spinal levels, for example C5 and T1 on the front of the arm.
Across such a line there is little overlap.
There is no cutaneous area supplied by C1

There is no cutaneous area supplied by C1, because the C1 nerve has no cutaneous branch.
The C2 dermatome reaches the vertex.
The posterior two-thirds of the scrotum is supplied by S3

The posterior two-thirds of the scrotum is supplied by S3 and the anterior third by L1, an example of an axial line in the perineum.
L1 via the ilioinguinal and genital branches.
Division of a single intercostal nerve produces a band of anaesthesia on the trunk

Because adjacent dermatomes overlap, division of a single intercostal nerve usually produces no anaesthesia, except across an axial line.
Answer C: 1, 2 and 3.
The biceps jerk is mediated by C5 and C6

The biceps jerk is mediated by C5 and C6. Triceps is C7, the knee jerk L3/4 and the ankle jerk S1.
These are the standard reflex levels.
The knee jerk is mediated mainly by L3 and L4

The knee jerk is mediated mainly by L3 and L4, through the femoral nerve to quadriceps.
It is reduced in L4 root lesions.
Extension of the great toe is a good test of the L5 myotome

Extension of the great toe (extensor hallucis longus) is a good test of the L5 myotome.
L5 has no reliable reflex.
The ankle jerk is mediated mainly by L4

The ankle jerk is mediated by S1 (and S2), not L4.
It is lost in S1 radiculopathy.

questions.s: Movements and their main segmental supply:
o: Shoulder abduction and lateral rotation, C5

Shoulder abduction and lateral rotation (deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor) are mainly C5.
So C5 lesions weaken shoulder abduction.
Hip flexion, L4 and L5

Hip flexion and adduction are mainly L2 and L3. Hip extension and abduction are L4 and L5.
Flexion is higher up.
Ankle plantarflexion, L4 and L5

Ankle plantarflexion is mainly S1 and S2. Dorsiflexion is L4 and L5.
"Push down = S1."
Knee extension, L5 and S1

Knee extension (quadriceps) is L3 and L4. Knee flexion is L5 and S1.
Answer A: 1 only.
The spinal dura is separated from the vertebral periosteum by an epidural space containing fat and veins

The spinal dura is separated from the vertebral periosteum by an epidural space containing fat and veins, unlike the cranial dura, which is fused to the periosteum.
That is why spinal epidural haematomas and abscesses can form.
The spinal dura is firmly attached to the margin of the foramen magnum

The spinal dura is firmly attached to the margin of the foramen magnum, and also to the backs of the bodies of C2 and C3 and the posterior longitudinal ligament.
Below that it is largely free.
The dural sleeves of the spinal nerves end at the dorsal root ganglia, becoming continuous with the epineurium

The dural sleeves of the spinal nerves end at the dorsal root ganglia, where the dura fuses with the epineurium at the intervertebral foramen.
So the subarachnoid space ends there too.
The subarachnoid space ends at the conus medullaris

The subarachnoid space extends to S2, below the conus, containing the cauda equina. This is the space sampled in lumbar puncture.
The cord ends higher, at L1/2.

questions.s: Concerning development and the vertebral column of the child:
o: The spinal cord ends at about L3 at birth

At birth the spinal cord ends at about L3. It ascends relatively to L1/2 as the vertebral column grows faster than the cord.
So lumbar puncture in neonates is done lower.
The cervical curvature becomes a secondary ventral convexity when the infant holds up its head

The cervical curvature, a secondary curve convex forward, develops when the infant holds up its head. The lumbar curvature develops when the infant starts to walk.
Secondary curves are postural.
The fetal vertebral column is C-shaped and concave ventrally

The fetal vertebral column is C-shaped and concave ventrally (the primary curvature), retained in the thoracic and sacral regions.
Primary curves are concave forward.
The nucleus pulposus is derived from sclerotome

The nucleus pulposus is notochordal. The vertebral bodies and annulus fibrosus come from sclerotome.
Answer C: 1, 2 and 3.
